title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services

reading.body:
Scammers used AI-generated deepfake videos and fake social media profiles to impersonate a real, named immigration attorney, then sold fraudulent legal services to immigrants. The failure mode is deliberate impersonation: AI tools were used outside any legitimate deployment context, as instruments of fraud rather than products of a company offering a service. The point of harm was social media platforms, where thousands of fake accounts operated long enough to reach victims before takedowns began.

The gap that allowed the scheme to persist was the absence of platform-level identity verification capable of detecting synthetic likenesses of real professionals at scale. Nearly 6,500 fake accounts were removed only after the real attorney hired a private anti-piracy firm, meaning the platforms' own detection did not stop the accounts proactively. A verification step tying professional credentials to accounts offering legal services would have raised the cost of this kind of impersonation.

What is not established is the identity of the perpetrators, the total number of victims, or whether any law enforcement investigation has produced findings.

reports.title: Scammers steal identity of renowned Miami attorney to target immigrants on social media
South Florida immigration attorney says AI scammers are using his identity to target immigrants
Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
Legal resident loses thousands seeking citizenship to AI immigration attorney

summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become the target of a widespread AI-generated scam targeting vulnerable immigrants. Criminals have created hundreds of fake social media profiles and videos using artificial intelligence to impersonate Leal and offer fraudulent immigration services. The scammers use deepfake videos to promote illegal residency assistance for payments ranging up to $2,200, with victims being directed to contact numbers through WhatsApp and sent fake contracts.

Leal discovered the scheme last October when potential clients began calling his office, but the fraud has escalated dramatically over the past three months. His team hired an anti-piracy company that removed nearly 6,500 fake accounts, including 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram. Leal has changed his personal phone number and plans to contact local and federal authorities to launch an investigation. He warns immigrants to watch for payment requests through apps like Venmo and Zelle, and to verify the identity of anyone offering legal services online.
